cues.text: Let's close this study session with a consolidation of the whole chapter.
Think of this as the checklist you should be able to work through on your own before an exam, so let's go through it in order.
First, the distinctions.
You must be able to tell apart continuous integration, continuous delivery, continuous deployment and DevOps.
Continuous integration is about merging code changes frequently and checking each one automatically, so that integration problems show up early.
Continuous delivery goes further: the software is kept in a state where it could be released at any time, but a person still decides when.
Continuous deployment removes that manual decision, so a change that passes every check is released automatically.
DevOps is wider than any of these.
It is the way development and operations work together, and the pipeline is one tool within it.
These definitions are my own plain-language framing of terms you have met in this chapter, so check them against your course notes when you revise.
Second, you should be able to draw a pipeline that includes tests, security checks and approval.
Picture it left to right.
A code change is committed, then built, then put through automated tests.
Security checks sit in the same flow, so a weakness is caught before release, not after it.
Then comes an approval step, where a person or a defined policy signs off.
Only after that does the change move toward release.
When you draw it, label each stage and show what happens when a stage fails: the change stops and goes back to the developer.
Third, a list of topics you must be able to explain.
Immutable artifacts: the thing you build once is the thing you deploy, unchanged, in every environment.
Infrastructure as code, or IaC: describing environments in versioned files instead of configuring them by hand.
Dependency risks: the libraries and packages you rely on can bring in weaknesses or breakages of their own.
Release management: planning and controlling how changes reach users.
Versioning: giving each release an identifiable number so everyone knows exactly what is running.
Deployment choices: the different ways of putting a release into production.
Canary metrics: the measurements you watch while a new version serves a small share of users, to decide whether to continue.
Rollback and data compatibility: being able to go back to the previous version, and recognising that if data has been changed in a way the old version cannot read, going back is not simple.
RPO and RTO: the recovery point objective and the recovery time objective, which concern how much data loss is tolerable and how quickly service must be restored after a failure.
And finally continuous improvement: using what you learn from each release and each incident to make the next one better.
The source lists these topics without further detail here, so for the full explanations, return to the earlier chapters of this session.
Now the principle that ties everything together, and it is worth remembering word for word: faster deployment requires better evidence, not bypassed gates.
Speed is not achieved by skipping tests, security checks or approvals.
It is achieved by automating them and trusting their results, so that each release arrives with stronger proof that it is safe.
If you can say that sentence and back it up with the topics above, you are well prepared.
